- Model consistently overestimates early in the forecast horizon, especially in the first 5–10 days, then underestimates later days.
- Forecasts tend to overshoot after sharp price spikes (e.g., 80+ levels), then sharply correct downward — model fails to capture the magnitude of the correction.
- Model exhibits persistent downward bias in the final 5–10 days of the 30-day forecast, suggesting mean reversion is not adequately modeled.
- Forecast errors are more severe in the middle of the horizon (days 10–20) — model struggles with volatility clustering or sudden drops.
- Model underestimates the rate of decline after a peak, especially when true outcome shows rapid downward momentum.
- Model tends to smooth out volatility — underestimates sharp drops and overestimates gradual declines.
- Forecasts often lag behind true price movements by 1–3 days, particularly in the first 10 days — model is slow to react to new information.
- Model fails to capture the “tail risk” of sudden drops — especially when true outcome drops below 60 after a peak above 75.
- Model overconfident in early forecast days — forecasts are too high relative to recent history, especially when recent prices are falling.
- Model underestimates the impact of policy or market events — when true outcome drops sharply, model doesn’t adjust downward quickly enough.
